questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what an approval process can do that a validation rule cannot?
options: An approval process can route a record to a human for a judgment-call decision; a validation rule can only block or allow a save based on data already present on the record.
An approval process can route a record to a human for a judgment-call decision; a validation rule can also route a record to a human by assigning its error message to a specific approver.
A validation rule can lock a record from editing while a decision is pending; an approval process has no way to lock a record at all.
An approval process only works on the Opportunity object, while validation rules can be created on every object in the org.
A validation rule evaluates a formula at save time; an approval process's entry criteria can never use a formula.
Both tools make exactly the same kind of decision automatically, so choosing between them is purely a matter of which Setup menu you'd rather use.
questions.explain: A validation rule can only say yes or no, instantly, from data already on the record — it cannot ask a human to look at something and decide. An approval process fills that gap: it locks a record and routes it to one or more people for an actual decision.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it correctly states the approval-process half, but then claims a validation rule can also route a record to a human — it cannot. A validation rule's only output is an error message blocking the save; it has no mechanism to send anything to an approver or wait for a response. That one claim is the error.

questions.prompt: This is an Opportunity validation rule's Error Condition Formula. A rep saves an Opportunity with Discount_Percent__c = 45 and a value already typed into Discount_Justification__c. What happens?
options: The save succeeds, because the formula evaluates to FALSE — the discount exceeds 40, but the justification field is not blank, so AND() needs both conditions true and only one is.
The save is blocked, because Discount_Percent__c alone exceeding 40 is enough to trigger the rule, regardless of what's in the justification field.
The save succeeds, because validation rules never actually block a save outright — they only log a warning for later review.
The save is blocked, because ISBLANK() returns TRUE whenever a field contains any text at all, not just when it's genuinely empty.
questions.explain: A validation rule's formula describes invalid data, and TRUE blocks the save. AND() requires both arguments to be true — Discount_Percent__c > 40 is true, but ISBLANK(Discount_Justification__c) is false since the field has text, so the whole formula is FALSE and the save goes through.

questions.prompt: A single approval step has two approvers assigned in parallel, set to "require unanimous approval." One approver rejects immediately; the other hasn't responded yet. Select every statement that correctly describes what happens, per Lesson 3.
options: The record is rejected, because unanimous approval requires every assigned approver to approve, and a single rejection stops the step.
The step waits indefinitely for the second approver's response before taking any action at all.
The second approver's eventual response, whatever it turns out to be, has no further effect once the rejection has already resolved the step.
The process automatically escalates the decision to the second approver's manager instead of using the original assignment.
If the second approver later approves, that approval overturns the earlier rejection and the record proceeds.
questions.explain: "Require unanimous approval" means every assigned approver has to approve, so a single rejection stops the step immediately — the record is rejected right then, and the second approver's response no longer changes that outcome.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the formula function ________(Discount_Justification__c) returns TRUE when that field has no value at all — the function Lesson 4's validation rule combines with AND() and a discount-percent comparison to require justification for large discounts.
questions.explain: ISBLANK(field) returns TRUE when a field has no value, which is exactly what the discount-justification validation rule checks before blocking a save on an unusually large, unexplained discount.

questions.prompt: Match each approval-process term to what it actually is.
right: Preventing edits to a record while it waits for an approval decision
A group of users who share responsibility for approving records, instead of one hard-coded person
A condensed, one-step wizard that applies Salesforce's suggested defaults
The full wizard, broken into named steps, that almost every real-world approval process needs
questions.explain: The Jump Start Wizard is the condensed, one-step wizard with defaults. The Standard Setup Wizard is the full, named-step wizard real processes actually need. A Queue lets any member act on a request instead of naming one person. Record locking prevents edits while a decision is pending.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of configuring and then using an approval process, per Lessons 2-3, in the order they actually happen.
items: Specify entry criteria so only qualifying records enter the process
Add one or more approval steps, each with its own step criteria and assigned approver
A user clicks Submit for Approval, locking the record
The Approval History related list logs each step's decision
questions.explain: Entry criteria and approval steps are configured before a process can be activated. Only after activation does Submit for Approval appear on a record; clicking it locks the record and starts routing, and every decision along the way lands automatically in Approval History.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes when validation rules run, relative to triggers, in Salesforce's documented order of execution for a record save?
options: Validation rules run after before-triggers execute, but still before the record is saved to the database.
Validation rules run after after-triggers execute, but still before the record is saved to the database.
Validation rules run before any trigger of any kind, so a before-trigger can never affect what the validation rule evaluates.
Validation rules only run the first time a record is ever saved, and never again on any later edit.
Validation rules run only when an admin manually clicks Check Syntax, never automatically on save.
Validation rules run after the record has already been committed to the database, as a final audit step.
questions.explain: The documented order runs before-triggers, then system validation and custom validation rules, then the record is saved. A before-trigger can normalize a value and the validation rule will see the normalized version — that's a deliberate design, not a quirk.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it also claims validation runs 'before the record is saved' — but after-triggers run after the record has already been saved to the database in the documented order, so a rule can't run after them and still be before the save. That one swapped word, before-triggers versus after-triggers, is the actual error.

questions.prompt: A workflow rule's field update fires on a record save. Per Lesson 9, what's the platform-enforced limit on how many extra times this can force the record to re-save itself?
options: It can only force one additional re-save — Salesforce does not let a workflow field update cascade beyond that single extra pass.
It has no limit at all; a workflow field update can keep re-triggering itself indefinitely until a governor limit error appears.
It can force exactly two additional re-saves before Salesforce blocks any further ones.
It never triggers an additional re-save; only Apex triggers and Flow can cause recursion.
questions.explain: Salesforce has a hard safeguard against the worst case: a workflow field update only re-triggers that one additional save, once. It will not cascade into an unbounded loop from workflow rules alone.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 7's checklist, select every situation that genuinely still calls for Apex rather than a declarative tool.
options: Processing large volumes of records with predictable, tested performance across deeply related records
A human needs to make a judgment call before a record is allowed to proceed
Integrating with an external system in a way that needs custom authentication or request/response shaping beyond Flow's built-in actions
The logic just evaluates some fields and returns a true/false or calculated value
Complex, deeply nested business logic that has to be provably correct, with automated test coverage
questions.explain: Bulk performance across related records, integrations beyond Flow's built-in actions, and logic needing provable correctness with real test coverage are exactly where Lesson 7 says Apex still earns its place. A human judgment call is an approval process's job, and simple field evaluation is a formula's job — neither needs code.

questions.prompt: An Apex trigger on Case updates a field on the same record it just processed, with no recursion guard written into it. What actually happens, per Lesson 9?
options: The trigger keeps re-firing on its own update until it hits a governor limit, which throws a runtime error the user sees as a failed save.
Salesforce automatically caps the trigger's self-triggered re-saves at exactly one extra pass, the same ceiling it applies to workflow field updates.
The second save is silently skipped, because Salesforce recognizes the trigger already ran once in this transaction.
The record saves successfully every time, because an Apex trigger is physically unable to update the record that invoked it.
questions.explain: Unlike workflow field updates, Apex triggers don't have a built-in recursion ceiling. A trigger that updates its own record without a guard genuinely can run until it hits a governor limit and throws an error — the fix is a recursion guard the developer has to build themselves.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 10, before permanently removing automation you believe is no longer needed, you should first ________ it rather than delete it outright, since that action can be reversed in seconds if something still depended on it silently.
questions.explain: Validation rules, approval processes, and workflow rules can all be deactivated without being deleted — turned off but still present, documented, and restorable in seconds. Deleting is permanent and destroys the configuration history.

questions.prompt: Harborline's quote approval process uses entry criteria of Discount_Percent__c > 10 instead of routing every submitted quote through both approval steps. Why does that matter, per Lesson 11?
options: It keeps quotes under the threshold out of the approval process entirely, so reviewers only see discounts large enough to actually need their judgment.
It has no real effect, since both approval steps would reject a quote under 10% anyway.
It only changes which email template is used, not whether the quote enters the process at all.
It determines how long the record stays locked, but not whether the record enters the process.
questions.explain: Entry criteria is the first line of defense: a quote under 10% never enters the process at all. Getting that condition right is cheaper than fixing it after reps start filing tickets about quotes that shouldn't have been routed to a manager in the first place.

questions.prompt: Briarcliff's SLA design uses two separate scheduled actions — a 1-hour warning and a 4-hour breach notice — off the same case, instead of one action firing once at the 4-hour mark. Why, per Lesson 12?
options: The warning and the breach notify different people with different messages, and firing the warning early gives the case owner a chance to act before anyone above them is looped in.
Salesforce's scheduled actions can only ever notify the record owner, so a second action was needed just to reach the manager.
A single scheduled action can only ever check one field, so a second action was required to also evaluate Priority.
The breach action immediately replaces the warning action, so only one of the two can exist on a case at any given time.
questions.explain: The warning fires at the three-hour mark specifically so the case owner still has an hour to act before a manager is notified — paging a manager the moment every Urgent case is created would train people to ignore the warning entirely. The breach step is a separate action with a separate audience.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, select every question that belongs in the five-question documentation template every piece of business process automation should answer.
options: What business problem does this automation solve, in one sentence?
Exactly what makes it fire, in plain language and in the actual logic?
Which Salesforce edition is the org currently running?
Which users, profiles, or record owners does it affect?
What other automation, fields, or processes does it depend on?
How many total lines does the formula take up?
Who owns it, and when was it last reviewed against reality?
questions.explain: The five questions are purpose, trigger/entry criteria, who it affects, dependencies, and owner/last-reviewed date. The org's Salesforce edition and a formula's line count don't appear anywhere in the template — they're not questions that help the next admin understand why the automation exists.

questions.prompt: Put these five stages of the Chapter 3 method, per Lesson 16's recap, in their correct order.
items: Translate the stakeholder complaint into plain-language requirements
Design the automation: entry criteria, steps, locking, final actions
Document it: purpose, trigger, who it affects, dependencies, owner
Test it across happy path, boundary, bulk, and negative cases
questions.explain: Skipping straight from translating the complaint to shipping is exactly how Harborline ended up with an undocumented, untested process in the first place — design, documentation, and testing aren't optional overhead, they're what makes shipping safe.

questions.prompt: A first draft of Harborline's entry criteria uses Discount_Percent__c >= 10 instead of > 10. What actually breaks, per Lesson 15's boundary-value testing?
options: A quote sitting at exactly 10% now silently enters an approval process it was never supposed to touch.
A quote at exactly 10% is silently excluded from approval, even though the business wanted it included.
Nothing changes, because >= and > behave identically when comparing a percentage field.
The approval process fails to activate at all until the operator is corrected.
questions.explain: Writing >= 10 instead of > 10 means a quote at exactly 10% now meets the entry criteria and enters approval — the opposite of what the boundary case was supposed to exclude. Boundary values are exactly where this kind of off-by-one mistake hides.

questions.prompt: Match each category of Lesson 15's test matrix to its definition.
right: Verifying automation behaves correctly when many records change in one transaction
Confirming automation correctly does NOT fire on a record it shouldn't touch
The obvious case the automation was built for
A test case sitting exactly at the edge of a condition, where off-by-one mistakes hide
questions.explain: Happy path is the obvious intended case. Boundary values sit exactly at a condition's edge. Bulk tests cover many records changing at once. Negative/edge tests confirm automation correctly stays silent on records it was never meant to touch.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder says "people are confused about time-off approval." Per Lesson 17, what's the risk of designing automation directly from that sentence without further discovery?
options: You might build something that addresses the vague symptom, like a reminder to clarify the process, instead of the actual root cause, like missing entry criteria.
There's no real risk — a stakeholder's first sentence always contains every detail needed to design entry criteria correctly.
The automation will simply fail to deploy until a formal written requirements document exists.
The risk only applies to approval processes, never to validation rules or scheduled actions.
questions.explain: Designing straight from the symptom risks building something that fixes the wrong thing. Discovery questions are what turn "people are confused" into the specific root cause — no entry criteria exists at all — that an actual design can target.

questions.prompt: Select every discovery question Lesson 17 recommends asking before designing automation for a new stakeholder complaint.
options: What exactly triggers the problem, with an actual number or condition rather than a vague description?
Who should be involved, specifically, by named role rather than "someone in management"?
What color should the approval button be on the record's page layout?
Are there exceptions, like emergency cases or different rules by department?
How will we know this is fixed, in a measurable outcome?
questions.explain: Lesson 17's discovery questions surface the exact trigger, the specific role involved, any exceptions, and a measurable definition of success. A page layout's button color isn't a requirements question at all.

questions.prompt: Mapping Mill Creek's time-off process surfaces a gap that a requirements list alone, stating only "requests over 5 days need approval," might leave ambiguous. What is that gap, per Lesson 18?
options: Whether a request of 5 days or fewer is auto-approved with no review, or needs some other explicit handling, since the list never states what happens on that branch.
Whether the manager approver should be a queue instead of an individual, which the requirements list already states clearly.
Whether validation rules run before or after triggers, which has nothing to do with this particular process.
Whether Harborline's discount approval and Mill Creek's time-off approval are built on the same Salesforce object.
questions.explain: A process map forces an explicit answer for every branch, including the one nobody explicitly asked about — what happens to a short request. A requirements list that only states the over-5-days condition can leave the under-5-days path ambiguous; the map makes that gap visible.
